data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject when the test's failure is a recorded, irreversible event in the installation record, and describes it when the test's failure is not recorded or is reversible. The 3-of-26 result is explained by the fact that only the shown-to-fail-first mutation in compile.py has a recorded failure event in the installation history; every other module's guards have no recorded failure, so their failures, if any, were folded back into the code without leaving a trace, making the guards indistinguishable from descriptions.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If an ordinarily-guarded module has a recorded failure event and still loses 4/4 to 6/7 mutations, the record-based mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the shown-to-fail-first mutation's failure was not recorded but the mutation was still lost, the mechanism's necessity is disproven.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a guard with no recorded failure rejects a mutation because the mutation changes the code's interface, the mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Constraint requires a durable record of rejection. When a test fails and the failure is recorded, the subsequent code change is constrained by the need to satisfy the recorded failure. When a test fails but the failure is not recorded, the author can adjust either the code or the test without accountability, and the test becomes a description of whatever the code does after the adjustment. The installation record is the mechanism that converts a transient failure into a lasting constraint, and the absence of such records in the ordinarily-guarded modules is why their mutation losses are high.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
